newsitem.title: UK: UK's Labour, Conservatives trade tax jibes.
newsitem.headline: UK's Labour, Conservatives trade tax jibes.

text.p: The Conservatives and the opposition Labour party on Tuesday traded accusations about tax policy, each accusing the other of hitting voters' pockets.

In a carefully-staged media launch, deputy prime minister Michael Heseltine and Conservative party chairman Brian Mawhinney unveiled a new poster which said a Labour government would increase taxes by 2,300 pounds per household.

But in a bid to upstage the event, Labour's campaign manager Brian Wilson unveiled a seven-foot-high model bomb in front of the Conservative poster with a slogan accusing the government of boosting taxes by 2,120 pounds per household since 1992.
Both sides, doggedly trading charges in the pre-election doldrums until Major announces the election date, accused the other of using distorted figures.
"We're contrasting the tax increases which a real family is paying with the fantasy figures the Tories (Conservatives) are saying," Wilson told reporters.

But Heseltine, dismissing Wilson's charges that the ruling party's figures were "fantasy", said: "They (Labour) have got 30 billion pounds worth of outstanding (spending) pledges, so where's the money coming from?"

Heseltine and Mawhinney also criticised Labour in the wake of its failure to win a Monday night vote to censure Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg. If Labour had won, it could have prompted a no-confidence vote, but the government survived by 13 votes.
Heseltine said the victory "It gives a very welcome support to the Prime Minister's determination to keep his nerve and continue to let the economy improve".

Labour has said it will keep up the pressure on Major, although deputy leader John Prescott said the party would wait and see what happened after a by-election later this week before deciding whether to stage another parliamentary challenge.
The government currently has 322 seats in the Commons, exactly the same number as all the other parties combined.
But it will dip into a minority if, as expected, Labour wins the February 27 by-election in Wirral South, north-west England.

Major does not have to call an election until May 22, although his favoured date is believed to be May 1. Monday night's vote calmed speculation that he might be forced into calling an election earlier. -- London Newsroom +44-171-542-7768
